opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as two halves of the same thing, and for a long time people treated them as separate. The model is the brain: reasoning, knowledge, the ability to generalize. The agent framework is more like the body and the environment, the hands, the memory, the tools, the feedback loop that lets the brain actually do things in the world and learn from what happens.

If you look at how humans become intelligent, it's not just that we have a powerful brain sitting in a jar. We act, we make mistakes, we get feedback, we use tools, we write things down, we collaborate. Intelligence emerges from that interaction. So if we only scale the model and never give it a rich way to act and receive feedback, I think we hit a ceiling. And if we build very elaborate agent frameworks on top of a weak model, then the framework is just a lot of scaffolding compensating for missing capability. It becomes brittle. Every new task needs new hand-written rules.

What I find exciting right now is that the boundary is moving. A lot of things we used to engineer into the framework, like planning, reflection, deciding when to call a tool, are increasingly being learned by the model itself, especially through reinforcement learning in real environments. The framework becomes thinner and more general, and the model internalizes more of the agentic behavior. So in some sense, the framework is a temporary place where we put the abilities the model hasn't learned yet.

But I don't think the framework disappears entirely. The environment, the tools, the long-term memory, the interfaces to the real world, those will always matter, just like humans still need computers and notebooks even though we're smart. So my view is: the model should own the intelligence, and the agent framework should provide the world it learns from and acts in. Getting the co-design right, training the model inside the same kind of environment it will be deployed in, is probably one of the most important paths toward something closer to human-like intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the model and the framework are not two separate things competing for credit. They are two layers of the same system, and right now the division of labor between them is shifting fast.

A few years ago, the model was essentially a very good next-token predictor, and the agent framework did almost all the heavy lifting. You had to hand-write the planning loop, the tool-calling logic, the memory, the retry strategies, the reflection step. The framework was compensating for what the model could not do on its own. That is why there were so many agent frameworks, and why most of them were brittle. You were encoding a lot of human intuition about how reasoning should proceed into fixed scaffolding.

What has changed is that more and more of that scaffolding is being absorbed into the model itself. Once you train a model with reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, with real tools and real feedback, the model learns when to plan, when to call a tool, when to back off and re-examine an assumption. Those behaviors stop being things you wire in from the outside and become things the model does natively. So in a sense, the model is eating the framework from the inside.

But I do not think the framework disappears. I think its role changes. The framework stops being a substitute for intelligence and becomes the environment in which intelligence operates. It handles things that are genuinely external to the model: persistent memory across sessions, access control, sandboxing, verification, coordination between multiple agents, the interface to the real world. Those are not things you want the model to improvise. Those are the body and the nervous system, while the model is the brain.

The analogy I like is that humans also do not reach intelligence with a brain alone. We have culture, tools, institutions, writing. A huge amount of what we call human intelligence lives outside any single skull. So when people ask whether human-like intelligence comes from the model or from the agent framework, I think the question slightly misframes it. The intelligence comes from the whole loop: a model that can reason and learn from feedback, embedded in an environment that gives it memory, tools, and consequences.

Where I would push back on some of the industry is the belief that you can get there by clever orchestration alone. If the base model does not have strong reasoning and good judgment about uncertainty, no framework will rescue it. You will just get a very elaborate way of making mistakes faster. The core capability has to come from training. The framework amplifies it, grounds it, and makes it safe to deploy, but it cannot manufacture it.

So my view is that the real research frontier is at the boundary between the two. How do you design training signals that teach a model to use an environment well? How do you design environments that expose the model to the kinds of feedback that actually improve its judgment? When those two things co-evolve, that is when you start to see behavior that looks less like a chatbot with plugins and more like something that is genuinely working toward a goal over time.

astra-6.text:
I think the model’s capabilities and the agent framework need to develop together. The model provides the ability to understand, reason, and generalize. The framework lets it put those abilities to work: use tools, maintain context, act in an environment, and learn from feedback.

But I wouldn’t assume that wrapping a model in a sufficiently elaborate framework gets us to human-like intelligence. If the model can’t reliably handle an unfamiliar situation, a workflow may help with particular tasks without resolving that underlying limitation.

The interesting question is what should be learned by the model and what should be handled by the surrounding system. As models become stronger, some things we currently engineer into frameworks may become capabilities of the model itself. So I see that boundary as moving, rather than as a fixed division.

sol-6.1.text:
I think models and agent frameworks operate at different levels. The model provides capabilities such as understanding, reasoning, and learning, while the framework connects those capabilities to tools, memory, and feedback from an environment.

A framework can help a model accomplish much more, but completing a task through a carefully designed workflow doesn’t necessarily mean the model has acquired a general ability. We need to distinguish what the model can reliably understand from what the surrounding system makes possible.

For human-like intelligence, I would expect both to matter. Stronger models make agents more adaptable, and interaction through agents can provide experiences that help models improve. The interesting question is how to turn that experience into transferable learning, so the system becomes better at unfamiliar problems instead of only executing familiar workflows.
